title: Enhancing Clinical Decision Support and Differential Diagnosis with Knowledge Graphs, and Retrieval Augmented Generation in Generative AI
summary: Diagnostic error carries a burden, while unconstrained large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to hallucination and weak integration of quantitative laboratory dynamics. We developed a decision-support pipeline combining disease-specific biomarker correlation graphs, ordinary differential equations (ODEs), deep sequence classification, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). For 103 disease classes from a full blood count (FBC) repository, biomarker networks were used as coupling matrices to generate 30 trajectories per disease (3,090 total). A one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) and long short-term memory (LSTM) network classified disease trajectories and six dynamical clusters. A constrained GPT-4o-mini RAG layer used a 19-pattern BMJ Best Practice/NICE corpus to generate differential diagnoses evaluated for diagnostic suitability, evidential grounding, and clinical plausibility. Across five random-seed runs, disease-level accuracy was $0.940 \pm 0.006$ for the CNN (95\% CI 0.933--0.948) and $0.852 \pm 0.019$ for the LSTM (95\% CI 0.828--0.875); the CNN advantage was 8.87 percentage points (95\% CI 6.47--11.27; $t(4)=10.26$, $p=5.1\times10^{-4}$; Hedges' $g=3.67$). Among 100 sampled RAG cases, 96 parsed successfully; evidence was cited in 97.9\%, the true diagnosis was mentioned in 71.9\%, and the composite score was 3.82/5 with a 47.9\% strict pass rate. The central finding was a decoupling between grounding and diagnostic correctness: classifier-correct versus classifier-wrong outputs differed in diagnostic suitability but not evidential grounding. Post-hoc analysis confirmed a 1.02-point diagnostic-score difference (Mann--Whitney $p=0.0024$; Hedges' $g=0.72$), whereas grounding differed by only $-0.02$ points ($p=0.839$; $g=-0.04$).

AI.tldr: The paper presents a decision-support pipeline combining biomarker correlation graphs, ODEs, deep sequence classification (CNN/LSTM), and RAG to diagnose 103 full blood count disease classes, achieving 94% CNN accuracy and revealing a decoupling between RAG evidential grounding and diagnostic correctness.
AI.motivation: Diagnostic errors pose a significant burden to healthcare, while unconstrained LLMs are prone to hallucination and fail to integrate quantitative laboratory dynamics (e.g., time-series blood count changes).
AI.method: The pipeline uses disease-specific biomarker correlation graphs as coupling matrices within ODEs to generate 30 trajectories per disease for 103 disease classes. A 1D CNN and LSTM classify disease trajectories and six dynamical clusters, followed by a constrained GPT-4o-mini RAG layer using a 19-pattern BMJ/NICE corpus to generate differential diagnoses evaluated for suitability, grounding, and plausibility.
AI.result: CNN achieved 0.940±0.006 disease-level accuracy (95% CI 0.933–0.948), outperforming LSTM (0.852±0.019) by 8.87 percentage points (p=5.1×10⁻⁴; Hedges' g=3.67). Among 100 RAG cases, 96 parsed; evidence cited in 97.9%, true diagnosis in 71.9%, composite score 3.82/5 with 47.9% strict pass rate. Key finding: classifier-correct vs. wrong outputs differed in diagnostic suitability (1.02-point difference, p=0.0024) but not evidential grounding (−0.02 points, p=0.839).
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates strong classification performance and reveals that evidentiary grounding in LLM-generated diagnoses is decoupled from actual diagnostic correctness, highlighting a critical limitation of grounding-based evaluation as a proxy for diagnostic accuracy in AI decision support.

title: A mechanistic modeling framework to interpret ACTH stimulation tests across HPA axis adaptation states and glucocorticoid feedback dynamics
comment: 11 pages, 1 Table, 6 Figures; Matches the version published in Computers in Biology and Medicine
summary: The hypothalamic pituitary adrenal (HPA) axis is a key regulatory system coordinating endocrine responses to physiological and psychological stress. While the ACTH stimulation test remains a cornerstone of adrenal function assessment, its interpretation is complicated by the dynamic and adaptive nature of the HPA axis under chronic stress exposure. In particular, prolonged stress induces glandular remodeling, glucocorticoid receptor (GR) resistance and delayed feedback recovery, all of which may alter test outcomes without indicating primary adrenal failure. In this study, we present a mechanistic modeling framework that integrates hormonal kinetics, feedback inhibition and functional mass adaptation of the corticotroph and adrenal compartments. We simulate the HPA axis over $180$ days encompassing three phases - baseline, chronic stress and recovery, while introducing a time varying GR resistance function to mimic feedback desensitization and its resolution. Using this framework, we evaluate both low dose ($1 μg)$ and high dose ($250 μg)$ ACTH stimulation tests across physiological phases. Our simulations show that cortisol responses are highly sensitive to both the magnitude and timing of stress exposure and that ACTH responsiveness is phase dependent and often blunted during recovery due to persistent feedback resistance. Low dose ACTH testing more reliably reflects partial adrenal adaptation, while high dose tests risks masking dysfunction due to supraphysiological drive. These results highlight the limitations of static testing paradigms and suggest that accounting for glandular plasticity and GR feedback dynamics is essential for effective endocrine diagnosis particularly in stress related or treatment induced adrenal disorders.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a mechanistic computational model of the HPA axis that simulates 180 days of chronic stress exposure and recovery, incorporating glandular remodeling and glucocorticoid receptor (GR) resistance. The model evaluates both low-dose (1 μg) and high-dose (250 μg) ACTH stimulation tests across physiological phases, showing that cortisol responses are phase-dependent and that low-dose testing better reflects partial adrenal adaptation while high-dose testing can mask dysfunction.
AI.motivation: The interpretation of ACTH stimulation tests is complicated by the dynamic, adaptive nature of the HPA axis under chronic stress. Prolonged stress induces glandular remodeling, GR resistance, and delayed feedback recovery, which can alter test outcomes without indicating primary adrenal failure—highlighting the need for a mechanistic understanding of these dynamics.
AI.method: A mechanistic modeling framework integrating hormonal kinetics, feedback inhibition, and functional mass adaptation of corticotroph and adrenal compartments. The HPA axis is simulated over 180 days across three phases (baseline, chronic stress, recovery) with a time-varying GR resistance function to mimic feedback desensitization. Both low-dose (1 μg) and high-dose (250 μg) ACTH stimulation tests are evaluated across these phases.
AI.result: Simulations show cortisol responses are highly sensitive to the magnitude and timing of stress exposure, and ACTH responsiveness is phase-dependent—often blunted during recovery due to persistent feedback resistance. Low-dose ACTH testing reliably reflects partial adrenal adaptation, while high-dose tests risk masking dysfunction due to supraphysiological drive.
AI.conclusion: Static testing paradigms have limitations for assessing adrenal function under dynamic stress conditions. Accounting for glandular plasticity and GR feedback dynamics is essential for effective endocrine diagnosis, particularly in stress-related or treatment-induced adrenal disorders.

title: Slow-Fast Brain-Computer Interfaces: Preventing Neuroadaptive Overfitting in AI-Mediated Neural Interfaces
comment: Commentary, 1 figure, 1 table, 12 pages including references
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) from task-specific neural decoders into adaptive systems that complete language, smooth movement, regulate rehabilitation support and adjust stimulation. These capabilities can increase speed, fluency, usability and clinical reach, yet conventional performance metrics may overlook losses in intent fidelity, authorship, agency, therapeutic challenge and durable clinical benefit. I define neuroadaptive overfitting as a closed-loop failure mode in which an AI-mediated BCI becomes over-optimized to short-term proxies of success, including reduced effort, rapid acceptance, lower workload or smooth task completion, while drifting from the user's durable goals. I then propose Slow-Fast BCI, a framework for pacing AI assistance according to decoder evidence, uncertainty, contextual and clinical stakes, fatigue, and user- or clinician-defined goals. The framework distinguishes fast assistance when intent is clear and stakes are low, guarded assistance under uncertainty and slow assistance when misalignment could compromise safety, agency, authorship, motor learning or therapeutic value. Across communication, motor-control, neurorehabilitation and closed-loop neuromodulation applications, I outline corresponding safeguards and evaluation measures. This Perspective argues that AI-mediated BCIs should be evaluated not only by decoding accuracy and task performance, but also by how AI assistance is deployed: when systems act autonomously, seek confirmation, preserve user effort or return control to the user.

AI.tldr: This Perspective introduces the concept of "neuroadaptive overfitting" in AI-mediated brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), where systems become over-optimized to short-term performance proxies (e.g., reduced effort, fast acceptance) at the expense of durable user goals. The author proposes the "Slow-Fast BCI" framework that paces AI assistance based on decoder evidence, uncertainty, stakes, and user-defined goals, distinguishing between fast, guarded, and slow assistance modes. The paper argues that AI-mediated BCIs should be evaluated not only by accuracy and task performance but also by how AI assistance is deployed regarding autonomy, confirmation, effort preservation, and user control.
AI.motivation: Conventional performance metrics for AI-based BCIs may overlook critical losses in intent fidelity, authorship, agency, therapeutic challenge, and durable clinical benefit as these systems evolve from simple neural decoders into adaptive, autonomous clinical tools.
AI.method: The paper defines neuroadaptive overfitting as a closed-loop failure mode where BCIs over-optimize short-term proxies of success and drift from durable user goals. It introduces the Slow-Fast BCI framework, which categorizes AI assistance into three paces—fast (clear intent, low stakes), guarded (uncertainty), and slow (high misalignment risk)—based on decoder evidence, contextual/clinical stakes, and user-defined goals, with corresponding safeguards across communication, motor control, neurorehabilitation, and neuromodulation.
AI.result: The paper outlines safeguards and novel evaluation measures for each assistance pace across four BCI application domains, arguing that evaluation must move beyond decoding accuracy and task performance to include how assistance is deployed.
AI.conclusion: AI-mediated BCIs should be assessed on how AI assistance is deployed—autonomy levels, confirmation seeking, effort preservation, and control return—rather than only on traditional performance metrics, to protect user agency and durable clinical benefit.

title: A greedy nearest-neighbor approach to quantify site revisitation: comparing two sympatric raven species
summary: A central challenge in movement ecology is to describe ecologically meaningful residence sites from raw tracking data due to heterogeneous sampling frequency and uncertain site boundaries. Here, we develop a greedy nearest-neighbor clustering approach with local reassignment and polygon-based site construction that generates timestamped sequences of site visits for each tracked individual, and apply it to nine years of GPS data from two sympatric raven species in the Dead Sea region---the Fan-tailed raven (\emph{Corvus rhipidurus}) and the Brown-necked raven (\emph{C. ruficollis}). Using the resulting visitation sequences, we quantify recursion patterns using the non-Markovian individual mobility model (IMM), which captures the balance between novel-site discovery $β$ and preferential return $α$. The inferred dynamics are consistent with IMM predictions and reveal clear interspecific differences: Brown-necked ravens continue to discover new sites at a higher rate (lower $β$), whereas Fan-tailed ravens show a steeper concentration of visits among top-ranked sites. Entropy analyses further separate the species, with Brown-necked ravens exhibiting higher site entropy and higher conditional entropy of site-to-site transitions. Together, these results provide a robust framework for describing interspecific differences in movement strategies that can be used to infer memory from GPS data and suggest distinct space-use strategies in two closely related sympatric species.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a greedy nearest-neighbor clustering approach with local reassignment and polygon-based site construction to identify residence sites from raw GPS tracking data, then applies it to nine years of data from two sympatric raven species to quantify recursion patterns using the individual mobility model (IMM), revealing distinct interspecific differences in movement strategies.
AI.motivation: A central challenge in movement ecology is describing ecologically meaningful residence sites from raw tracking data due to heterogeneous sampling frequency and uncertain site boundaries.
AI.method: Greedy nearest-neighbor clustering with local reassignment and polygon-based site construction to generate timestamped sequences of site visits; recursion patterns quantified using the non-Markovian individual mobility model (IMM) capturing novel-site discovery (beta) and preferential return (alpha); entropy analyses on site usage and transitions.
AI.result: The inferred dynamics are consistent with IMM predictions and reveal clear interspecific differences: Brown-necked ravens discover new sites at a higher rate (lower beta) while Fan-tailed ravens show steeper concentration of visits among top-ranked sites; entropy analyses separate the species with Brown-necked ravens showing higher site entropy and higher conditional transition entropy.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a robust method for describing interspecific differences in movement strategies, useful for inferring memory from GPS data, and suggests distinct space-use strategies in two closely related sympatric species.

title: Mutation--selection balance on an infinite trait space: confinement, drift and equilibrium
summary:
We study a trait-structured population model incorporating mutation, selection and density-dependent regulation on a countably infinite trait space. The underlying stochastic process is a continuous-time Markov chain in which individuals reproduce at a trait-independent rate, offspring traits are determined by a mutation kernel on $\mathbb Z$, mortality depends on trait, and births are progressively suppressed as the population approaches a fixed population ceiling. Using results for density-dependent Markov population processes with countably many types, we derive a deterministic approximation in the form of an infinite system of nonlinear differential equations.
  We establish existence and positive invariance of solutions, and investigate the equilibrium structure of the deterministic system. A fundamental distinction emerges between bounded and confining mortality profiles. When mortality remains bounded, mutation may continually transport mass through the trait space and a stationary trait distribution need not exist. In contrast, when mortality increases without bound as the absolute value of the trait index becomes large, the operator $L=D^{-1}P$, where $P$ and $D$ govern mutation and mortality, is compact. By combining compactness with Kreĭn-Rutman theory for compact positive operators on Banach lattices, we show that $L$ has an algebraically simple principal eigenvalue with a strictly positive eigenvector, and we derive a threshold condition for the existence of a non-zero equilibrium. In this regime the equilibrium is unique, and its trait distribution is determined by the principal eigenvector of $L$. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results and illustrate the contrasting behaviours associated with bounded and confining mortality profiles.

AI.tldr: A trait-structured population model with mutation, selection, and density regulation on an infinite trait space is studied. Under confining (unbounded) mortality profiles, compactness and Krein-Rutman theory yield a unique non-zero equilibrium determined by the principal eigenvector of a mutation-mortality operator; under bounded mortality, stationary distributions may not exist.
AI.motivation: To understand how mutation, selection, and density-dependent regulation interact on an infinite trait space, and to determine when stationary trait distributions exist and are unique—fundamental questions that depend critically on whether mortality is bounded or grows without bound.
AI.method: The population is modeled as a continuous-time Markov chain on a countably infinite trait space. Deterministic approximation is derived via an infinite system of nonlinear ODEs using density-dependent Markov population process results. Existence and positive invariance of solutions are established. Compactness of the operator L=D^{-1}P is shown for confining mortality, and Krein-Rutman theory for compact positive operators on Banach lattices is applied to characterize eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and equilibrium thresholds.
AI.result: For bounded mortality, mutation can continually transport mass and no stationary trait distribution need exist. For confining mortality, L has an algebraically simple principal eigenvalue with a strictly positive eigenvector, a threshold condition for existence of a non-zero equilibrium is derived, and the equilibrium is unique with trait distribution determined by the principal eigenvector. Numerical experiments confirm these contrasting behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The mortality profile qualitatively determines the fate of the population: bounded mortality can prevent stationary trait distributions from forming, whereas confining mortality guarantees a unique non-zero equilibrium whose shape is governed by the principal eigenvector of the compact operator L. This provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for trait-structured evolutionary dynamics on infinite trait spaces.

title: Neural Logic, Invariance, and the Retina---McCulloch and Pitts
comment: Book chapter from NeuroAI: Theoretical Foundations of Dynamics, Learning and Computation in Brains, Minds, and Machines. Includes reproducible figures and accompanying code
summary: This chapter reconstructs the McCulloch-Pitts program as a physics of neural computation rather than the familiar cartoon of a binary neuron. The 1943 logical calculus is developed in both directions: given a net, characterize the propositions realized by its activity; given an admissible logical expression, construct a net that realizes it. We recover the original distinction between thresholded excitatory summation and absolute inhibitory veto-one the weighted-threshold form cannot preserve for arbitrarily large excitatory inputs-and read unit-time delay as the physical realization of logical depth. Recurrence is treated exactly: an autonomous, deterministic network of finitely many binary units has a finite state space, so every trajectory eventually enters a periodic orbit-a fact about finite-state dynamics, not unbounded Turing computation. A single threshold element realizes only linearly separable Boolean functions, whereas finite feedforward networks of them synthesize any Boolean function on a finite domain. We then follows McCulloch and Pitts beyond threshold logic. The 1945 heterarchy paper turns cyclic preference into an obstruction to representation by a scalar utility. The 1947 work on universals asks how a physical network can identify inputs related by nuisance transformations, developed here via group averaging and feedback canonicalization. The 1959 frog-retina study makes the adequate-stimulus question experimental, revealing parallel invariant operations before the brain proper. Spike-triggered analysis shows how a nonlinearly driven neuron can have a vanishing first-order average while second-order statistics recover its hidden selectivity: methodological failure can masquerade as physiological absence. Modern mathematical tools are used without projecting their notation onto the historical papers, and limitations of the idealization are stated explicitly.

AI.tldr: This chapter reinterprets the McCulloch-Pitts program as a physics of neural computation, developing their 1943 logical calculus in both directions (net→propositions and expression→net), examining threshold vs. inhibitory logic, exact recurrence dynamics, and extending through their later works on heterarchy, universals, and the frog-retina study—using modern mathematical tools without anachronistic projection.
AI.motivation: To correct the oversimplified "binary neuron" cartoon of McCulloch-Pitts and recover the full depth of their original program as a genuine physics of neural computation, including distinctions (like veto vs. weighted-threshold inhibition) that the standard caricature loses.
AI.method: The paper reconstructs the McCulloch-Pitts framework by: (1) developing the 1943 logical calculus bidirectionally (analysis of nets and synthesis of nets from logical expressions); (2) treating recurrence as finite-state dynamics with periodic orbits; (3) analyzing the computational expressiveness of single threshold elements vs. finite feedforward networks; (4) tracing the program forward through the 1945 heterarchy, 1947 universals (via group averaging and feedback canonicalization), and 1959 frog-retina papers; (5) employing spike-triggered analysis to reveal how nonlinear neurons can hide selectivity in first-order statistics while revealing it in second-order statistics.
AI.result: The analysis recovers the original veto-vs-weighted-threshold distinction that cannot be preserved for arbitrarily large excitatory inputs, reads unit-time delay as physical logical depth, establishes that recurrent networks produce periodic orbits (not unbounded computation), shows single threshold elements realize only linearly separable functions while feedforward networks synthesize any Boolean function, and demonstrates that methodological failures (vanishing first-order averages) can masquerade as physiological absences in neural analysis.
AI.conclusion: The McCulloch-Pitts program is best understood as a physics of neural computation with both logical and physical dimensions, whose conceptual distinctions and limitations remain relevant; modern tools should be used carefully without projecting contemporary notation onto the historical work, and the idealization's limitations must be stated explicitly.

title: Mus siliconus: A Neuro-Musculoskeletal Digital Twin of the Mouse Integrating Neural Dynamics, Biomechanics, and Tactile Sensing
summary:
Digital twin technologies could transform neuroscience and biomedicine by creating predictive computational representations of living organisms. However, most animal digital twins model neural circuits, anatomy, or biomechanics separately rather than integrating the processes that generate behavior. We argue that animal digital twins should instead be conceived as embodied dynamical systems that unify neural activity, body mechanics, sensory feedback, and environmental interactions.
  We propose a neuro-musculoskeletal digital twin of the mouse that combines multimodal anatomical reconstruction from X-ray CT, high-resolution white-light sections, and Scx-GFP imaging with biomechanical simulation, Bonhoeffer--van der Pol neural dynamics, and tactile feedback. This framework forms a closed sensorimotor loop in which behavior emerges through continuous interactions among the nervous system, musculoskeletal system, and environment. The Bonhoeffer--van der Pol model provides a computationally tractable dynamical foundation for large-scale simulation of these interactions.
  Neuro-musculoskeletal digital twins could provide a convergence point for computational neuroscience, biomechanics, artificial intelligence, and robotics. When coupled with adaptive learning and autonomous experimentation, they may develop from passive simulations into active scientific instruments that generate hypotheses, predict interventions, and guide experiments. Such embodied digital twins could advance the study of biological intelligence and support new adaptive biomedical and robotic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes that animal digital twins should be conceived as embodied dynamical systems integrating neural activity, body mechanics, sensory feedback, and environmental interactions. The authors propose a neuro-musculoskeletal digital twin of the mouse combining multimodal anatomical reconstruction, biomechanical simulation, Bonhoeffer–van der Pol neural dynamics, and tactile feedback in a closed sensorimotor loop, with the potential to evolve into active scientific instruments.
AI.motivation: Most current animal digital twins model neural circuits, anatomy, or biomechanics in isolation rather than integrating the processes that generate behavior. The authors argue this fragmented approach fails to capture the embodied nature of biological intelligence and motivates the need for unified digital twin frameworks.
AI.method: The proposed framework is a neuro-musculoskeletal digital twin of the mouse combining multimodal anatomical reconstruction (X-ray CT, high-resolution white-light sections, and Scx-GFP imaging) with biomechanical simulation, Bonhoeffer–van der Pol neural dynamics, and tactile feedback. These components form a closed sensorimotor loop where behavior emerges from continuous interactions among the nervous system, musculoskeletal system, and environment.
AI.result: The paper presents a conceptual and architectural framework rather than empirical results, demonstrating that the Bonhoeffer–van der Pol model provides a computationally tractable dynamical foundation for large-scale simulation of neuro-musculoskeletal interactions, enabling embodied behavior emergence.
AI.conclusion: Neuro-musculoskeletal digital twins could serve as a convergence point for computational neuroscience, biomechanics, AI, and robotics. When coupled with adaptive learning and autonomous experimentation, they may progress from passive simulations into active scientific instruments that generate hypotheses, predict interventions, and guide experiments, advancing the study of biological intelligence and supporting new biomedical and robotic systems.

title: Subcellularly Resolved Single-Cell Embedding Learning with Transcriptomic data, Protein Structure and Localization Information
summary: Existing cell embedding methods predominantly rely on transcriptomic or proteomic measurements and represent each cell as a holistic entity, thereby overlooking the subcellular localization of individual molecules. Moreover, they rarely incorporate protein structural information, despite its fundamental role in determining molecular interactions and functions. In this work, we propose a multimodal framework for learning subcellularly resolved cell embeddings by jointly leveraging RNA expression profiles, protein sequence representations, and protein structural information. Specifically, we employ a cross-attention architecture to integrate transcriptomic, sequence, and structural modalities and model their interactions within distinct subcellular compartments. The resulting embeddings represent each cell through its fine-grained subcellular organization, capturing both molecular expression patterns and the functional properties of the associated proteins. By learning cell representations at subcellular resolution, our framework preserves spatially organized biological information while integrating complementary signals across multiple molecular levels. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first framework that produces subcellularly resolved cell embeddings by jointly incorporating transcriptomic information, protein sequence representations, and protein structural knowledge within a unified cross-modal learning paradigm.

AI.tldr: A multimodal framework that learns subcellularly resolved cell embeddings by jointly integrating RNA expression, protein sequence representations, and protein structural information using a cross-attention architecture across distinct subcellular compartments.
AI.motivation: Existing cell embedding methods treat cells as holistic entities and overlook subcellular localization of molecules, while rarely incorporating protein structural information despite its importance in molecular interactions and functions.
AI.method: A cross-attention architecture integrates three modalities—transcriptomic, protein sequence, and protein structural—to model their interactions within distinct subcellular compartments, producing fine-grained subcellular cell representations.
AI.result: The framework produces cell embeddings that capture subcellular organization along with molecular expression patterns and functional properties of associated proteins, preserving spatially organized biological information through multi-level integration.
AI.conclusion: This is the first framework to produce subcellularly resolved cell embeddings by jointly incorporating transcriptomic data, protein sequence representations, and protein structural knowledge within a unified cross-modal learning approach.

title: Fungal Memory and Minimal Cognition
summary: This paper argues that fungal mycelial networks exhibit minimal cognition through memory-integrated adaptive regulation. Drawing on cybernetic and enactivist frameworks, I develop a non-representational account of memory as the organism's capacity to modulate behavior based on temporally extended environmental coupling. I propose four operational criteria for minimal cognition: feedback-guided regulation of behavior, maintenance of internal viability conditions, structural modulation based on past environmental interactions, and plasticity across time scales that supports anticipatory adaptivity. Empirical evidence demonstrates that fungi meet all four criteria through distributed memory mechanisms: fungal networks exhibit directional regrowth toward previously encountered resources even after spatial displacement; stress priming persists across multiple cell divisions; Spitzenkörper-mediated directional persistence in constrained environments; and transgenerational memory through spore imprinting. These findings challenge representationalist assumptions in cognitive science by showing that memory and cognition can emerge from morphodynamic, biochemical, and electrophysiological processes without necessary neural substrates or symbolic representations. Fungal cognition demonstrates that the organizational principles underlying cognition - feedback-driven adaptation, norm-preservation, and historical coupling - can be realized in radically different material substrates, expanding our understanding of what counts as a cognitive system.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that fungal mycelial networks exhibit minimal cognition through memory-integrated adaptive regulation, proposing four operational criteria for minimal cognition and providing empirical evidence that fungi meet all four criteria through distributed memory mechanisms, challenging representationalist assumptions in cognitive science.
AI.motivation: To challenge representationalist assumptions in cognitive science by demonstrating that minimal cognition and memory can emerge from non-neural, morphodynamic processes in radically different material substrates like fungal networks.
AI.method: The author develops a non-representational account of memory grounded in cybernetic and enactivist frameworks, proposes four operational criteria for minimal cognition (feedback-guided regulation, maintenance of internal viability, structural modulation from past interactions, and plasticity supporting anticipatory adaptivity), and evaluates empirical evidence from fungal biology against these criteria.
AI.result: Empirical evidence demonstrates that fungi meet all four criteria through distributed memory mechanisms including directional regrowth after spatial displacement, stress priming persisting across cell divisions, Spitzenkörper-mediated directional persistence, and transgenerational memory via spore imprinting.
AI.conclusion: Fungal cognition shows that core organizational principles of cognition—feedback-driven adaptation, norm-preservation, and historical coupling—can be realized in non-neural substrates without symbolic representations, expanding what counts as a cognitive system.

title: Beyond species area curves: a theoretical approach to the relationship between diversity and area
summary: Species area curves, which describe the number of species present as a function of area, have long been used to understand biodiversity and inform conservation efforts. While understanding the number of species is important, it leaves out information about the population sizes of each species. In this work, we examine the relationship between the effective number of species from different diversity indices, like Simpson's index and the Shannon index, and area. These effective number of species are also referred to as Hill numbers. Using a spatial and neutral model that has previously been used to understand species area curves, we show through a combination of theory and simulations that the relationship between the effective number of species and area is linear when the area is sufficiently large and resembles a power law for smaller areas.

AI.tldr: This paper extends species-area curve analysis to effective number of species (Hill numbers like Simpson's and Shannon indices), showing through theory and simulations of a spatial neutral model that the relationship between effective species counts and area is linear for large areas but resembles a power law for smaller areas.
AI.motivation: Traditional species-area curves only count the number of species present in an area, neglecting information about population sizes of each species. The authors aim to incorporate diversity indices (effective number of species or Hill numbers) into the species-area relationship to provide a richer understanding of biodiversity patterns.
AI.method: Using a spatial and neutral model (previously applied to understand species-area curves), the authors combine theoretical derivations with simulations to analyze the relationship between effective number of species (from diversity indices like Simpson's and Shannon indices) and area.
AI.result: The relationship between effective number of species and area is linear when the area is sufficiently large and resembles a power law for smaller areas.
AI.conclusion: The effective number of species (Hill numbers) exhibits an area-dependence pattern that transitions from a power-law regime for small areas to a linear regime for large areas, providing a more nuanced view of biodiversity across spatial scales than traditional species-area curves.

title: 3D hybrid cellular Potts model with a discrete deformable fiber network: modeling cell contraction and extracellular matrix remodeling
comment: In revision for Biomechanics and Modeling in Mechanobiology
summary: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a fibrous and dynamic network that plays a critical role in development, homeostasis, and disease. Cells both respond to and remodel the ECM, engaging in a mechanical reciprocity that shapes tissues. To study these interactions, computational models have been developed that simulate either ECM mechanics or cell behavior. The Cellular Potts Model (CPM) is a flexible cell-based framework that has been extended to many biological processes, including coupling to a discrete deformable fiber network. So far, however, this extension has only been applied in two dimensions, even though a three-dimensional setting is biologically more relevant. Here, we present a 3D hybrid framework that couples the CPM with a discrete and deformable representation of the ECM. This model enables explicit simulation of cell-induced ECM remodeling, including fiber reorientation and matrix densification. By incorporating contractile forces through static adhesion points, the model captures how ECM elasticity and fiber stiffness influences cell shape. The simulations show that ECM stiffness, controlled by fiber crosslinking, resists contraction and reaches equilibrium, while crosslink density modulates fiber alignment and local matrix accumulation. This framework provides a versatile platform for studying cell-ECM mechanics and supports future studies of multicellular behavior in realistic 3D environments.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a 3D hybrid computational framework that couples the Cellular Potts Model (CPM) with a discrete deformable fiber network to simulate cell-induced extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, including fiber reorientation and matrix densification, demonstrating how ECM stiffness and crosslink density influence cell shape and matrix organization.
AI.motivation: Cells and the ECM exhibit mechanical reciprocity critical for tissue function, but existing computational models coupling cell behavior to ECM mechanics have only been implemented in 2D, which is biologically less relevant than a 3D setting.
AI.method: A 3D hybrid framework is developed that couples the Cellular Potts Model (CPM) with a discrete, deformable representation of the ECM fiber network. Contractile forces are incorporated through static adhesion points, allowing simulation of cell-induced ECM remodeling such as fiber reorientation and matrix densification.
AI.result: Simulations show that ECM stiffness, controlled by fiber crosslinking, resists cell contraction and reaches equilibrium. Additionally, crosslink density modulates fiber alignment and local matrix accumulation, and the model captures how ECM elasticity and fiber stiffness influence cell shape.
AI.conclusion: This 3D framework provides a versatile platform for studying cell-ECM mechanics and supports future investigations of multicellular behavior in realistic three-dimensional environments.

title: An adaptive time-tree transition kernel for Bayesian phylogenetic inference
summary: Bayesian phylogenetic and phylodynamic analyses can be very time-consuming, owing to the combination of complex models that are used to estimate key parameters from increasingly large genomic data sets and their associated metadata. The use of high-performance computer hardware can -- to a certain extent -- alleviate the computational burden and markedly decrease the time to results. Still, even converging to the posterior can be a lengthy endeavour, with the burn-in aspect of such analyses potentially taking days or even weeks for large data sets. One of the key aspects that hampers performance in Bayesian phylogenetic inference is the efficiency with which tree topology proposals explore tree space. We here propose a novel adaptive tree transition kernel, which we call `subTreeLeap' (STL), which involves modifying the phylogeny by walking along patristic distance paths in the tree according to an adaptable radius parameter. STL is a general proposal, which can be used with contemporaneous or time-calibrated sequence data, being particularly suited to the latter due to respecting temporal precedence constraints. We carefully assess its impact on convergence and statistical mixing of the exploration of posterior tree space, by comparison to replicate ``golden runs'' obtained from lengthy analyses of empirical data under standard tree transition kernels. We find that STL successfully explores the same posterior tree space as standard kernels, but often does so in a more efficient manner. We discuss limitations as well as future potential improvements to STL that could substantially increase the speed at which Bayesian phylogenetic inferences are obtained.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel adaptive tree transition kernel called 'subTreeLeap' (STL) for Bayesian phylogenetic inference, which modifies phylogenies by walking along patristic distance paths with an adaptable radius parameter. STL is shown to explore the same posterior tree space as standard kernels but more efficiently, particularly suited for time-calibrated data.
AI.motivation: Bayesian phylogenetic and phylodynamic analyses are computationally expensive and time-consuming, especially with large genomic datasets. The burn-in phase can take days or weeks. A key bottleneck is the efficiency of tree topology proposals in exploring tree space during MCMC sampling.
AI.method: The authors introduce subTreeLeap (STL), an adaptive tree transition kernel that modifies phylogenies by walking along patristic distance paths according to an adaptable radius parameter. STL is a general proposal compatible with both contemporaneous and time-calibrated data (particularly suited to the latter due to respecting temporal precedence constraints). Its performance is assessed by comparing convergence and statistical mixing against replicate 'golden runs' from lengthy analyses under standard kernels on empirical data.
AI.result: STL successfully explores the same posterior tree space as standard tree transition kernels, but often does so more efficiently in terms of convergence and statistical mixing.
AI.conclusion: STL offers a promising improvement for speeding up Bayesian phylogenetic inference. The authors discuss limitations of the approach and outline future enhancements that could substantially increase computational efficiency.

title: Prediction emerges in RNNs trained for perception
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, 2 supplementary figures. Code and fitted weights at https://github.com/qtabs/BayesPlusBach
summary: The brain is highly proficient at making sense of noisy and ambiguous sensory inputs. Predictive processing hypothesises that this ability relies on prediction. However, it is unclear why the brain would have evolved to predict the sensory world, a computationally expensive process, in order to aid perception. Here we use simulations to argue that prediction naturally emerges in systems optimised for perception. We train recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to denoise a tokenised version of Bach's compositions at a range of noise levels. Afterwards, we enquire whether the states of the networks contain predictive information about the next token. We test this by freezing the RNN weights and training a linear readout from its states on prediction. We compare the performance of the linear readout with that of an independently trained linear benchmark model. The results show that the linear readout from the RNNs outperforms the benchmark model at moderate levels of noise, indicating that the networks rely on a predictive mechanism to support perception. We further show that the responses of the RNNs to sensory inputs are proportional to prediction error. Together, the results demonstrate that neural signatures of predictive processing emerge, without any further training constraints, from optimisation of perception.

AI.tldr: The paper uses simulations with recurrent neural networks trained to denoise Bach compositions to argue that predictive processing naturally emerges from optimizing perception, without explicit training for prediction. Networks trained for denoising show predictive information about future tokens (outperforming a linear benchmark at moderate noise levels) and exhibit responses proportional to prediction error, suggesting predictive processing is an emergent byproduct of perception optimization.
AI.motivation: Predictive processing theory suggests the brain makes sense of noisy sensory inputs via prediction, but it is unclear why evolution would favor the computationally expensive process of prediction for aiding perception. The paper aims to explain whether prediction can emerge naturally from systems simply optimized for perception.
AI.method: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are trained to denoise a tokenized version of Bach's compositions across various noise levels. After training, network weights are frozen, and predictive information about the next token is tested by training a linear readout from network states on prediction. This is compared against an independently trained linear benchmark model. Network responses to sensory inputs are also analyzed for proportionality to prediction error.
AI.result: The linear readout from the RNN states outperforms the benchmark model at moderate noise levels, indicating the networks use a predictive mechanism to support perception. Additionally, RNN responses to sensory inputs are proportional to prediction error, showing neural signatures of predictive processing.
AI.conclusion: Neural signatures of predictive processing emerge naturally from optimization of perception alone, without any further training constraints, suggesting prediction may arise as an inherent consequence of building systems that perceive well rather than requiring explicit evolutionary or training pressure toward prediction.

title: Higher-order rich clubs and configuration models on general directed hypergraphs
comment: 31 pages, 15 figures, 2 tables, 4 supplementary figures, 1 supplementary table
summary: Detecting structure in complex networks, especially those arising from physical systems, is a central problem across the sciences. One approach is via rich club analysis, which identifies important vertices using a centrality metric and measures whether those vertices are more tightly interconnected than expected by chance. While informative, this approach captures only pairwise interactions, missing out on higher-order ones known to shape the structure and function of many complex systems. We propose a hyper-rich club pipeline that asks whether central vertices are more tightly interconnected than expected by chance through hyperedges encoding higher-order interactions, which also enables the inclusion of important, often omitted, directional information. We work in a broad class of hypergraphs, which we call general directed hypergraphs, that includes as special cases undirected hypergraphs, head-and-tail directed hypergraphs, and totally ordered hypergraphs (a hypergraph related to directed simplicial complexes from topological data analysis). This unifies several non-equivalent notions of directed hypergraph under one definition. On these hypergraphs we define a hyper-rich club framework whose concrete construction depends on explicit choices the domain scientist fixes according to their research goals. Particular choices recover the existing rich club notions for graphs and undirected hypergraphs, and yield the first such notion for each version of directed hypergraphs. We demonstrate that the pipeline recovers meaningful structure in data by studying networks of very different origins: connectomes, temporal networks of infectious spread, networks of poems, and the XGI hypergraph database, in each case detecting structure the standard graph rich club misses.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a hyper-rich club pipeline for detecting higher-order structure in complex networks encoded as general directed hypergraphs, unifying multiple directed hypergraph definitions and revealing meaningful structure in datasets ranging from connectomes to temporal infection networks that standard graph-based rich club analysis misses.
AI.motivation: Rich club analysis is a powerful tool for detecting structure in complex networks, but it only captures pairwise interactions, missing higher-order interactions that shape the structure and function of many physical and complex systems. Additionally, directional information in interactions is often overlooked.
AI.method: The authors propose a hyper-rich club pipeline based on a broad class of hypergraphs called general directed hypergraphs, which subsumes undirected hypergraphs, head-and-tail directed hypergraphs, and totally ordered hypergraphs. They define a hyper-rich club framework whose concrete construction depends on choices the domain scientist fixes, and particular choices recover existing rich club notions while yielding first such notions for each directed hypergraph version.
AI.result: The pipeline recovers meaningful structure across diverse datasets — connectomes, temporal networks of infectious spread, networks of poems, and the XGI hypergraph database — detecting structure that standard graph rich club analysis fails to find.
AI.conclusion: Higher-order rich club analysis via general directed hypergraphs provides a unified and flexible framework that captures structure invisible to pairwise-only rich club methods, with broad applicability across disciplines.

title: Omega-N: Interpretable Structural Node Descriptors and Their Applicability Domain
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures. Reference implementation, notebooks and data-preparation scripts at https://github.com/BiomeMakers/OmegaN
summary:
A composite structural index summarises a network in one number; for a triangle-based index it is spectrally redundant: Tr(A^3) is the third moment of the adjacency spectrum. The non-redundant content sits one level down, in diag(A^3), which depends on eigenvectors and is not spectrally determined. A corollary in the theory paper for this index family stated that, and predicted: the global scalar should tie sharpened spectral baselines rather than beat them, while the node-wise attribution should do better where the number of structural epicentres is unknown. This paper tests it.
  We construct Omega-N by localizing each of the four factors. The direct localization is badly conditioned; two corrections from published practice fix it, a configuration-null excess for every local factor and a personalized-PageRank neighbourhood at several scales, giving ten interpretable features per node from the graph alone, with no attributes, training or embeddings.
  Against a recursive feature engine at five levels of recursion, Omega-N wins on one and ties on four of six in-domain node-classification evaluations, with ten features against up to 252. Two statistics computed from the graph and labels, not from performance, partition the eight benchmarks without error, and the two they exclude are the two it loses.
  The strongest application is drug-target prioritisation on protein interaction networks: +0.073 to +0.144 AUPRC over a centrality battery across four constructions, replicated on an independent AP-MS network and label source, surviving three bias controls (degree-matched, ten repetitions: +0.1047 and +0.1030, both 10/10, p=0.00195). The clearest negative sits in the same application: adding Omega-N to centralities plus Node2Vec changes nothing (+0.0014, p=0.31). The claim is narrow: ten interpretable features

AI.tldr: The paper tests a theory prediction about triangle-based composite structural indices (which are spectrally redundant at the global Tr(A^3) level but informative at the diag(A^3) level). The authors construct Omega-N by localizing four factors with two correction techniques, producing ten interpretable features per node without attributes, training, or embeddings. Omega-N wins on one and ties on four of six in-domain node-classification benchmarks against a recursive feature engine (10 features vs up to 252). Its strongest result is in drug-target prioritization on protein interaction networks (+0.073 to +0.144 AUPRC over centrality baselines, replicated across independent networks and bias controls), though adding Omega-N to Node2Vec+centralities provides no improvement.
AI.motivation: To empirically test a theoretical prediction that global triangle-based structural indices should tie (not beat) spectral baselines, while node-wise attribution should perform better when the number of structural epicentres is unknown.
AI.method: Constructs Omega-N by localizing four spectral factors of diag(A^3), using a configuration-null excess correction and personalized-PageRank multi-scale neighbourhoods, yielding ten interpretable features per node from graph structure alone.
AI.result: Omega-N wins on one and ties on four of six in-domain node-classification benchmarks using only 10 features vs up to 252; achieves +0.073 to +0.144 AUPRC over centrality batteries in drug-target prioritization, replicated across independent networks and surviving degree-matched bias controls (p=0.00195), but adds nothing when combined with Node2Vec features.
AI.conclusion: The claim is intentionally narrow: ten interpretable, structure-only features can match or beat much larger feature sets in node classification and substantially improve drug-target prioritization over centrality baselines, but do not complement embedding-derived features.

title: Inverse planning of social interactions in relationships
summary: We propose a formal account of how structured, shared knowledge about social relationships shapes action interpretation. The model represents relationships as constraints in a social environment, analogous to boundaries or obstacles in a physical environment and operating within the same generative model, but exerting distinct constraints on action. As an initial test of this framework, we draw on research across the social sciences to capture in the models how one dimension of relationships -- formality versus intimacy -- shapes how people interpret interpersonally vulnerable behavior. We test this account in stories of naturalistic everyday situations, extending structured models of action understanding to open-ended contexts. Across six preregistered experiments (N = 1,554), the model captures people's inferences about desires, physical environments, and social relationships. This work formalizes how relationships can constrain -- and be revealed through -- everyday action.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a formal account of how structured, shared knowledge about social relationships shapes action interpretation, modeling relationships as constraints in a social environment analogous to physical boundaries yet exerting distinct constraints on action. Tested across six preregistered experiments (N=1,554) in naturalistic everyday stories, the model captures people's inferences about desires, physical environments, and social relationships, particularly showing how formality versus intimacy shapes interpretation of interpersonally vulnerable behavior.
AI.motivation: To provide a formal, computational account of how social relationships — as structured, shared knowledge — constrain and reveal action interpretation, extending structured models of action understanding from physical environments to the social domain.
AI.method: The model represents social relationships as constraints within a generative model, analogous to physical boundaries/obstacles, but with distinct action constraints. It draws on social science research to encode formality versus intimacy as a key relational dimension, and is tested on naturalistic everyday stories in six preregistered experiments.
AI.result: Across six preregistered experiments (N=1,554), the model successfully captures people's inferences about desires, physical environments, and social relationships in naturalistic, open-ended everyday contexts.
AI.conclusion: This work formalizes how social relationships can constrain — and be revealed through — everyday action, unifying social and physical constraints within a single generative framework of action understanding.

title: CliffRank: A Dual-Branch Framework for Activity-Cliff Ranking Prediction
summary: Activity-cliff ranking remains difficult because local structural changes can cause large activity differences, while high-quality data that resolve the underlying mechanisms remain limited. To use available activity labels more effectively, we combine absolute-activity regression with ranking-consistency learning. CliffRank trains two parallel predictors with mean squared error, a thresholded listwise loss, and Pairwise Preference Consistency (PPC), which aligns relative ordering in the preference-probability space. On three antimicrobial peptide datasets, CliffRank with ESM2-t12 achieved the highest mean Spearman correlation of 0.5393 and mean Recall@50 of 21.4, although the leading method varied across individual datasets. On three small-molecule datasets, CliffRank with PNA, where PPC was activated after 120 epochs, achieved the highest mean Spearman correlation of 0.6890, while its mean Recall@50 of 30.4 matched that of ACANet-PNA. The PPC results also define its practical limits. Asymmetric initialization improved the MolCLR-GIN averages but did not improve every target. For PNA without pretrained weights, delayed PPC improved selected metrics, but no schedule was best for both mean Spearman correlation and mean Recall@50. Future work should evaluate more targets and antimicrobial peptide systems, develop adaptive PPC schedules, and incorporate protein or membrane context when available.

AI.tldr: CliffRank combines absolute-activity regression with ranking-consistency learning to improve activity-cliff ranking, achieving the highest mean Spearman correlation of 0.5393 on antimicrobial peptide datasets and 0.6890 on small-molecule datasets.
AI.motivation: Activity-cliff ranking is difficult because local structural changes can cause large activity differences, and high-quality data resolving underlying mechanisms is limited, motivating more effective use of available activity labels.
AI.method: CliffRank trains two parallel predictors using mean squared error, a thresholded listwise loss, and Pairwise Preference Consistency (PPC) which aligns relative ordering in the preference-probability space. It employs ESM2-t12 for peptide datasets and PNA for small-molecule datasets, with PPC activated after 120 epochs and asymmetric initialization.
AI.result: On three antimicrobial peptide datasets, CliffRank with ESM2-t12 achieved the highest mean Spearman correlation of 0.5393 and mean Recall@50 of 21.4. On three small-molecule datasets, CliffRank with PNA achieved the highest mean Spearman correlation of 0.6890, with mean Recall@50 of 30.4 matching ACANet-PNA.
AI.conclusion: PPC defines practical limits for ranking improvement; future work should evaluate more targets and antimicrobial peptide systems, develop adaptive PPC schedules, and incorporate protein or membrane context when available.

title: Interpretable Symptom Vectors for Depression in a Large Language Model
summary: Patients with depression present with diverse symptom profiles, yet clinical practice routinely reduces this variation to a single severity score. Large language models (LLMs) can potentially capture various symptoms and their severity from patient speech. However, how depressive symptoms are represented inside LLMs remains poorly understood, limiting clinical trust. To examine whether internal model activations match clinician judgment, we analyzed the residual stream of Gemma-3-27B-PT using mechanistic interpretability techniques. Recording activations across symptom descriptions drawn from validated clinical instruments, we found that symptom groups geometrically separated the most at layer 21 across multiple distance metrics. Using Semantic Projection, we then projected held-out naturalistic text onto Symptom Vectors constructed from these instruments. The resulting per-symptom coefficients preserved clinician-annotated rank ordering across mood, somatic, and suicidality axes. Furthermore, a single depression vector in Layer 21 separates held-out depressive from non-depressive text (AUC = 0.789), which can be used as an emotional valence gate that restricts symptom projection to depressive speech. These results reveal a decorrelated, clinician-aligned symptom signal readable directly from internal activations, offering a mechanistic foundation for interpretable depression-assessment tools.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether internal activations of a large language model (Gemma-3-27B-PT) encode depressive symptoms in a way that aligns with clinician judgment. Using mechanistic interpretability, the authors find symptom groups separate most cleanly at layer 21, and demonstrate that Semantic Projection onto Symptom Vectors preserves clinician-annotated rank ordering across mood, somatic, and suicidality axes. A single depression vector achieves AUC = 0.789 in separating depressive from non-depressive text and can serve as an emotional valence gate for symptom projection.
AI.motivation: Depression is heterogeneous in symptom presentation, yet clinical practice reduces this to a single severity score. While LLMs could potentially capture diverse symptoms from patient speech, how depressive symptoms are represented internally within LLMs is poorly understood, which limits clinical trust and interpretability.
AI.method: The authors performed mechanistic interpretability analysis on the residual stream of Gemma-3-27B-PT. They recorded activations across symptom descriptions from validated clinical instruments, identified layer 21 as the point of maximal geometric separation between symptom groups using multiple distance metrics, constructed Symptom Vectors via Semantic Projection, and projected held-out naturalistic text onto these vectors. They also constructed a single depression vector as an emotional valence gate.
AI.result: Symptom groups showed the greatest geometric separation at layer 21. Per-symptom coefficients from projected naturalistic text preserved clinician-annotated rank ordering across mood, somatic, and suicidality axes. A single depression vector at layer 21 separated depressive from non-depressive text with AUC = 0.789.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal a decorrelated, clinician-aligned symptom signal that is directly readable from internal LLM activations, providing a mechanistic foundation for building interpretable depression-assessment tools.

title: Adversarial Vulnerabilities of Neural Biomarker Identification Systems
summary: There is growing interest in the proposed use of EEG signals as biometric credentials, but thus far there has been little research on the reliability and security of such biometrics. Prior adversarial tests have focused on deep-learning classifiers and assumed attackers have full access to the classifier model. This has left unexamined other, more popular categories of neural signature methods as well as the more realistic case of an adversary having only black-box access to a classifier. In this paper we develop a collection of adaptive attack algorithms which learn to fool an authentication system via targeted alterations of stolen EEG recordings, without requiring any knowledge of the authentication system itself. Tested on 6 public datasets spanning three recording conditions (reacting to visual stimuli, imagining hand movements, and resting), it reveals that different signaturing approaches vary significantly in their degrees of vulnerability to adversarial attacks. We show that vulnerability to spoofing attack is greatly impacted by the recording conditions, with significant variation depending on task at time of recording. Finally, we provide recommendations for improving neural signature biometrics based on the results of our adversarial testing.

AI.tldr: This paper develops black-box adaptive attack algorithms that fool EEG-based biometric authentication systems by modifying stolen EEG recordings, testing them across 6 public datasets and multiple recording conditions, revealing that vulnerability varies significantly by signaturing approach and recording task.
AI.motivation: Prior adversarial tests on EEG biometrics were limited to deep-learning classifiers with white-box (full model) access, leaving other classifier types and more realistic black-box attack scenarios unexamined.
AI.method: The authors develop a collection of adaptive attack algorithms that can fool an EEG authentication system via targeted alterations to stolen EEG recordings, operating without any knowledge of the authentication system (black-box access). They test this across 6 public datasets spanning three recording conditions: visual stimuli response, imagined hand movements, and resting state.
AI.result: Different neural signaturing approaches show significantly different degrees of vulnerability to adversarial attacks. The vulnerability to spoofing attacks is strongly influenced by recording conditions, with substantial variation depending on the task performed during recording.
AI.conclusion: Based on adversarial testing results, the authors provide recommendations for improving the security and reliability of neural signature biometrics.

title: Antipolar Cell-cell Adhesion-causing Collective Motility Disorder
summary: In this study, we aim to theoretically investigate antipolar cell-cell adhesion, in which adhesion sites are located on the opposite side of the leading edge of migrating cells, as a candidate for irregularly polarized adhesion that induces disorder in collective cell migration. We employ the cellular Potts model to simulate the effects of antipolar adhesion on collective migration driven by cell motility. Antipolar adhesion induces a collective motility disorder, which exhibits a disordered configuration in the motility direction, even when collective motion occurs in the absence of adhesion. Consequently, antipolar adhesion inhibits collective migration. The effect is in contrast to that of polar adhesion, which accelerates the directional intercellular order of cell motility. At a specific motility strength, a depinning transition emerges from a collective motility disorder to a collective motion. The collective motility disorder can be physically explained by the cooperative effect between antipolar adhesion and motility persistence within the mean-field approximation.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically investigates antipolar cell-cell adhesion (adhesion sites opposite the leading edge) as a mechanism for disorder in collective cell migration using the cellular Potts model. Antipolar adhesion induces collective motility disorder even when adhesion-free collective motion exists, thereby inhibiting collective migration—contrasting with polar adhesion which promotes directional order. A depinning transition from disorder to collective motion emerges at specific motility strength, and the disorder is explained via mean-field theory as a cooperative effect between antipolar adhesion and motility persistence.
AI.motivation: Collective cell migration is essential in biological processes, yet irregularities in polarization and adhesion can disrupt it. The authors aim to understand how antipolar cell-cell adhesion—a less-studied, irregular adhesive configuration—contributes to disordered collective migration, providing physical insight into mechanisms that inhibit coordinated cell movement.
AI.method: The study employs the cellular Potts model to simulate collective cell migration driven by cell motility, incorporating antipolar adhesion where adhesion sites are located on the side opposite the leading edge. A mean-field approximation is also used to physically explain the observed collective motility disorder.
AI.result: Antipolar adhesion produces a collective motility disorder characterized by disordered orientations of cell motility, suppressing collective migration. This contrasts with polar adhesion, which enhances directional intercellular order. A depinning transition from disorder to collective motion is observed at a specific motility strength. The collective disorder is attributed to a cooperative effect between antipolar adhesion and motility persistence within the mean-field framework.
AI.conclusion: Antipolar adhesion serves as a physical mechanism that disorders and inhibits collective cell migration, in direct opposition to polar adhesion. The findings reveal a depinning transition and provide a theoretical explanation based on the interplay between antipolar adhesion and motility persistence, deepening the understanding of how irregular cell adhesion patterns impair coordinated migration.

title: Memory as an Energy Landscape---Hopfield
comment: Book chapter from NeuroAI: Theoretical Foundations of Dynamics, Learning and Computation in Brains, Minds, and Machines. Includes reproducible figures and accompanying code
summary: This chapter reconstructs the Hopfield network as a physical theory of memory rather than merely an early neural-network algorithm. It begins with the problem as it stood before 1982-threshold logic, Hebbian association, correlation memories, and recurrent binary networks-and isolates what Hopfield's synthesis added: a dynamical definition of content-addressable memory, a symmetric recurrent architecture with a Lyapunov function, a Hebbian embedding of patterns in its couplings, and a physical account of basins, robustness, and graceful degradation. The binary and graded-response energy functions are derived in full, together with the signal-crosstalk decomposition governing pattern stability, the mean-field theory of retrieval at extensive load, and the zero-temperature retrieval spinodal at (alpha 0.138) established by Amit, Gutfreund, and Sompolinsky. The energy-based program is then followed through analog optimization networks, polynomial dense associative memories, exponential interactions, and modern continuous Hopfield updates, including the precise conditions under which the update becomes scaled dot-product attention. Throughout, capacity claims are tied to their disorder ensemble, scaling limit, and success criterion, showing why numerically different storage limits need not conflict. A closing assessment distinguishes established results from surviving principles, assumption-bound limitations, and open problems, treating the Hopfield network as an effective theory whose symmetry, locality, and point-neuron assumptions delimit its biological reach. Fixed-seed numerical experiments expose the mechanisms discussed but do not substitute for analytical results.

AI.tldr: This chapter reconstructs the Hopfield network as a physical theory of memory, deriving energy functions, stability conditions, and retrieval phase transitions, then tracing its evolution through modern extensions (including attention mechanisms) while carefully distinguishing established results from open problems.
AI.motivation: To reposition the Hopfield network from a historical neural-network algorithm into a rigorous physical theory of associative memory, clarifying what its 1982 synthesis uniquely contributed and reconciling apparently conflicting capacity claims across different formulations.
AI.method: The chapter provides full derivations of binary and graded-response energy functions, signal-crosstalk decomposition for pattern stability, mean-field theory of retrieval at extensive load, and the zero-temperature retrieval spinodal at alpha=0.138. It then traces the energy-based program through analog optimization, polynomial/exponential associative memories, and modern continuous Hopfield updates, tying capacity claims to their disorder ensembles, scaling limits, and success criteria. Numerical fixed-seed experiments supplement analysis.
AI.result: Establishes the precise conditions under which modern continuous Hopfield updates reduce to scaled dot-product attention, and demonstrates that numerically different storage limits across formulations need not conflict when properly contextualized by their disorder ensemble, scaling limit, and success criterion.
AI.conclusion: The Hopfield network should be treated as an effective physical theory whose symmetry, locality, and point-neuron assumptions delimit its biological reach. A closing assessment separates established results from principle-bound limitations and open problems, noting numerical experiments do not substitute for analytical results.

title: Seeing Beyond the Lesion: Disease Recognition from Reactive CNS Tissue
summary: Sampling error yields exclusively reactive, non-lesional brain parenchyma in a significant proportion of intracranial biopsies, leaving the underlying disease undiagnosed. We benchmark four pathology foundation models (UNI2-h, Virchow2, Prov-GigaPath, H-optimus-0) as frozen patch encoders within a shared attention-based multiple-instance learning framework using 245 whole-slide images from 186 patients with confirmed downstream diagnoses. We first show that coarse disease-category prediction can be reproduced largely from slide size alone. After restricting classification to three finer diagnostic distinctions within common tissue categories, this confound no longer explains performance, yet disease labels remain predictable above chance under permutation testing (p $\le 10^{-4}$ throughout). Surprisingly, performance is statistically indistinguishable across all foundation-model encoders, suggesting that recovering these weak morphological signatures is not limited by current patch representations. Signed instance-contribution maps and expert review further test whether predictive evidence localizes to reactive parenchyma rather than sampling-induced bias like blood introduced during tissue sampling. These results position acquisition-shortcut auditing via a provenance-only baseline as a necessary control in computational-pathology benchmarks, and show, once that confound is removed, that weakly supervised models still recover disease signal from tissue conventionally regarded as non-diagnostic.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether pathology foundation models can recover disease signals from non-lesional (reactive) brain biopsy tissue that would conventionally be deemed non-diagnostic. Using 245 whole-slide images from 186 patients, the authors benchmark four foundation model encoders within a shared multiple-instance learning framework, demonstrate that slide size alone confounds coarse disease prediction, and show that after removing this confound, fine-grained disease classification remains statistically significant. Notably, all four foundation models perform equally, suggesting the bottleneck is not patch representation quality.
AI.motivation: A significant proportion of intracranial biopsies yield only reactive, non-lesional brain parenchyma due to sampling error, leaving the underlying disease undiagnosed. The authors aim to determine whether weakly supervised models can still extract meaningful disease signal from tissue conventionally regarded as non-diagnostic, and to audit for acquisition-shortcut confounds (e.g., slide size, sampling-induced blood) that could inflate apparent performance in computational-pathology benchmarks.
AI.method: Four pathology foundation models (UNI2-h, Virchow2, Prov-GigaPath, H-optimus-0) are benchmarked as frozen patch encoders within a shared attention-based multiple-instance learning framework. The study uses 245 whole-slide images from 186 patients with confirmed downstream diagnoses, first establishing that coarse disease-category prediction can be reproduced from slide size alone (a confound), then restricting classification to three finer diagnostic distinctions. Permutation testing and signed instance-contribution maps with expert review are used to validate results and assess whether predictive evidence localizes to reactive parenchyma versus sampling-induced artifacts like blood.
AI.result: Coarse disease-category prediction is largely explained by slide size alone. After restricting to three finer diagnostic distinctions within common tissue categories, disease labels remain predictable above chance under permutation testing (p ≤ 10⁻⁴ throughout), with slide size no longer explaining performance. Performance is statistically indistinguishable across all four foundation-model encoders, indicating that recovering weak morphological signatures is not limited by current patch representations.
AI.conclusion: Acquisition-shortcut auditing via a provenance-only baseline should be a necessary control in computational-pathology benchmarks. Once the slide-size confound is removed, weakly supervised models can still recover genuine disease signal from tissue conventionally regarded as non-diagnostic, suggesting potential clinical utility for reactive parenchyma in intracranial biopsies.

title: A viscoelastic theory for ultrasound-induced intracellular streaming
summary: Ultrasound is increasingly used to control biological cells, but its multiple physical effects, including radiation force, streaming, heating, and cavitation, require theoretical frameworks that can quantify their relative strengths. Here we develop a semi-analytical model to predict flow patterns and energy distributions of ultrasound-induced intracellular streaming. Cells are modeled as viscoelastic droplets immersed in a fluid with different viscoelastic properties. For this geometry, the momentum equation with an Oldroyd-B constitutive law is solved using a perturbation expansion commonly applied in acoustofluidics. The resulting equations for the different orders of the expansion are solved using partial wave expansion and explicit integration. We investigate our model for a range of parameters which is relevant both for synthetic polymer and for protein solutions. We find a series of flow reversals that we can connect to the distribution of energy into the different modes. We also consider density and compressibility contrasts, which shift these transitions and introduce new ones. Finally, we discuss the potential biological relevance of our mathematical results for cellular sensing and signaling.

AI.tldr: A semi-analytical model is developed to predict flow patterns and energy distributions of ultrasound-induced intracellular streaming, treating cells as viscoelastic droplets in a viscoelastic fluid using Oldroyd-B constitutive law and perturbation/partial wave expansions. The model reveals flow reversals tied to energy mode distribution, influenced by density/compressibility contrasts, with implications for cellular sensing and signaling.
AI.motivation: Ultrasound is increasingly used to control biological cells, yet its multiple physical effects (radiation force, streaming, heating, cavitation) require theoretical frameworks capable of quantifying their relative strengths—particularly for intracellular streaming, which lacks adequate predictive models.
AI.method: Cells are modeled as viscoelastic droplets immersed in a fluid with different viscoelastic properties. The momentum equation with an Oldroyd-B constitutive law is solved using a perturbation expansion common in acoustofluidics, followed by partial wave expansion and explicit integration for equations of different expansion orders.
AI.result: The model finds a series of flow reversals connected to energy distribution into different modes. Density and compressibility contrasts shift these transitions and introduce new ones. The model is investigated across parameters relevant to synthetic polymer and protein solutions.
