AI.conclusion: The mathematical results are discussed in terms of their potential biological relevance for cellular sensing and signaling, suggesting the framework may provide insights into how ultrasound affects intracellular processes.

title: A Common Measure of Communication for Speech Brain-Computer Interfaces
comment: Code and OVMI Explorer available from the project page at https://neural-processing-lab.github.io/OVMI/
summary: Speech brain-computer interfaces (speech BCIs) translate neural activity into language, offering a path towards restoring speech for people with paralysis and, more broadly, enabling new forms of natural human-computer interaction. Despite this promise, the field lacks a common measure of progress because systems use different datasets, recording methods, types of speech, and vocabularies, so their reported scores are rarely comparable. Underlying this measurement problem are two unresolved questions: (i) what distribution of words should a speech BCI enable a user to communicate, and (ii) how much information from this distribution can a system convey. We address both by deriving open-vocabulary mutual information (OVMI), an information-theoretic quantity that measures the information conveyed by a decoder relative to a reference distribution over the words a user may wish to communicate. This allows capabilities measured under different conditions, such as distinct vocabularies, to be evaluated on a common communication scale. We show that ordinarily reported accuracy, word error rate (WER), and other metrics computed only over the words a system supports can overstate how much of a user's intended speech the system can communicate. We then use OVMI to compare existing systems, expose trade-offs between how much of the user's language a system supports and how accurately it decodes those words, show that these comparisons depend on what the user is expected to communicate, and demonstrate that selecting a vocabulary to maximise OVMI yields up to 16.3% relative improvement in accuracy across three speech domains. OVMI therefore provides the speech BCI community with a principled way to compare heterogeneous systems, improve vocabulary design, and measure progress in the field.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces open-vocabulary mutual information (OVMI), an information-theoretic metric that measures how much information a speech brain-computer interface (BCI) decoder conveys relative to a reference distribution of words users may wish to communicate. OVMI enables fair comparison of heterogeneous speech BCI systems across different vocabularies, recording methods, and datasets, and is shown to improve vocabulary selection by up to 16.3% relative accuracy improvement.
AI.motivation: The field of speech BCIs lacks a common measure of progress because systems use different datasets, recording methods, speech types, and vocabularies, making their reported scores incomparable. This measurement problem stems from two unresolved questions: what word distribution a speech BCI should enable, and how much information from that distribution a system can actually convey.
AI.method: The paper derives open-vocabulary mutual information (OVMI), an information-theoretic quantity that measures information conveyed by a decoder relative to a reference distribution over words a user may wish to communicate. This allows capabilities measured under different conditions (e.g., distinct vocabularies) to be evaluated on a common communication scale.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that traditionally reported metrics (accuracy, WER) computed only over supported words can overstate a system's communication capability. OVMI is used to compare existing systems, expose accuracy-vs-coverage trade-offs, and show comparisons depend on expected user communication. Selecting vocabularies to maximize OVMI yields up to 16.3% relative improvement in accuracy across three speech domains.
AI.conclusion: OVMI provides the speech BCI community with a principled way to compare heterogeneous systems, improve vocabulary design, and measure progress in the field on a common communication scale.
